frontier.hypothesis: Target's two LICM-hoisted constants (li 5 / li 20) precede the p-copy chain because in target's RTL they are NOT appended to the end of the loop preheader - they exist in the entry block with a LOWER INSN_LUID than `move t3,v0`, which makes them win the sched1 tie among priority-equal insns.
frontier.mechanism: loop.c hoists loop invariants by emitting them at the END of the preheader, which is why ours land last; sched1 then keeps them last because they have no in-block dependents (lowest INSN_PRIORITY) while `move t3,v0 -> move a2,t3` is a 2-deep chain. If instead the constants are materialized in the entry block by RTL generation or by CSE before the call's return copy, their LUIDs drop below the copies' and, with all of them priority-tied at the block end, LUID order decides - producing target's `li / li / move / move / lui / addiu / addiu`.
frontier.next_probe: Read the pre-loop block's per-insn INSN_PRIORITY and LUID directly. Session 3 left the exact blocker: tmp/grind/func_8003504C/s3/rank.sh runs the instrumented cc1 with BB2_RANK_DEBUG=1 (hook in rank_for_schedule, tools/gcc-2.7.2/sched.c) but its output is not scoped to one function and insn uids collide across code6cac_b.c's functions. Add a function filter (or bracket the dump per function) FIRST, then read the priorities of the seven pre-loop insns on the floor-4 form. If they are all priority-tied except the copy chain, the attack is to lower the constants' LUIDs; if the copy chain outranks them on priority, the attack is to give the constants an in-block dependent.

frontier.hypothesis: The pre-loop rotation is reachable by a DIRECTED permuter chassis (PERM_LINESWAP / PERM_GENERAL over the five init statements and over the order of the four disjuncts in loop 1's condition), even though undirected random search on the floor-4 chassis found nothing in 20k iterations.
frontier.mechanism: The order of the four disjuncts in `(u32)(lv-3) < 2 || (s8)lv == 5 || (u32)(lv-18) < 2 || (s8)lv == 20` sets loop.c's invariant DISCOVERY order and hence the order the two constants are appended to the preheader; the order of the five pre-loop init statements sets the entry block's LUIDs. Both are pure re-spellings of the same program, and neither has been swept on the floor-4 chassis (session 1 swept init order on the floor-24 chassis only, and session 4's own evidence is that chassis changes make an old sweep non-binding).
frontier.next_probe: Build a ws4 workspace from the floor-4 base.c with PERM_LINESWAP over the five init statements and PERM_GENERAL over the disjunct order, launch via `tools/permuter_campaign.py launch --label preloop-directed`, and cross-check any find with `sandbox --disable all`. Do NOT re-run undirected random on this chassis - 20373 iterations are already banked as a negative.

frontier.hypothesis: Cluster 1's remaining rotation is coupled to the `src`-reuse lever's exact placement, so sweeping WHERE the reused assignment sits (and which loop-2 pointer it feeds) can move the pre-loop block as well as the allocation.
frontier.mechanism: The `src = &D_801027D8;` statement is currently placed just before `D_800A38E1 = ...`, which is where the permuter happened to put it. Its position changes src's live range and the LUIDs of everything after it, and the allocation flip it produces already proved that this function's pre-loop scheduling and its allocation are coupled (session 1 recorded the same coupling in the other direction).
frontier.next_probe: Sweep the placement of `src = &D_801027D8;` across every legal point inside the `val == 5` branch (and the symmetric variant reusing `src` for dst_a instead of dst_d), measuring `sandbox --disable all` and the register dispositions for each. Cheap, mechanical, and it tests a premise no session has touched.
